claim: Neotropical manakin birds have evolved one of the fastest limb muscles on record to support innovations in acrobatic courtship display.
source: Previously, we found that Neotropical manakin birds have evolved one of the fastest limb muscles on record to support innovations in acrobatic courtship display (Fuxjager et al., 2016a).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Fuxjager et al., 2016a).

claim: Muscle specializations in manakins fostered divergence in courtship display speed, which may generate assortative mating.
source: Here, we show how this modification played an instrumental role in the sympatric speciation of a manakin genus, illustrating that muscle specializations fostered divergence in courtship display speed, which may generate assortative mating.
evidence: The claim is supported by data and analyses presented in the manuscript showing species differences in display speed and muscle performance.

claim: Innovations in contraction-relaxation cycling kinetics that underlie rapid muscle performance are punctuated by a severe speed-endurance trade-off.
source: However, innovations in contraction-relaxation cycling kinetics that underlie rapid muscle performance are also punctuated by a severe speed-endurance trade-off, blocking further exaggeration of display speed.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing that muscle relaxation declines with repeated stimulations at high frequencies.

claim: Sexual selection potentiated phenotypic displacement in a trait critical to mate choice during an extraordinarily fast species radiation.
source: Sexual selection therefore potentiated phenotypic displacement in a trait critical to mate choice, all during an extraordinarily fast species radiation—and in doing so, pushed muscle performance to a new boundary altogether.
evidence: The claim is supported by data on species divergence in display speed and muscle performance, combined with inference about the role of sexual selection.

claim: Bearded manakins last shared a common ancestor roughly 300,000 years ago.
source: This group last shared a common ancestor roughly 300,000 years ago (Brumfield et al., 2008; Tello et al., 2009), before splitting into four species: white-bearded manakins (M. manacus), golden-collared manakins (Manacus vitellinus), white-collared manakins (M. candei), and orange-collared manakins (M. aurantiacus).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to phylogenetic studies.

claim: Bearded manakins split into four species: white-bearded manakins, golden-collared manakins, white-collared manakins, and orange-collared manakins.
source: This group last shared a common ancestor roughly 300,000 years ago (Brumfield et al., 2008; Tello et al., 2009), before splitting into four species: white-bearded manakins (M. manacus), golden-collared manakins (Manacus vitellinus), white-collared manakins (M. candei), and orange-collared manakins (M. aurantiacus).
evidence: The claim is supported by established taxonomic knowledge and citations.

claim: Males produce the roll-snap behavior by rapidly hitting their wings together over their back, generating a mechanical trill-like sound.
source: Males produce this behavior by rapidly hitting their wings together over their back, generating a mechanical trill-like sound (Fuxjager et al., 2017a).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work describing the behavior.

claim: Repetitive rhythmic signals are a common signal type in animal courtship.
source: The result is a repetitive rhythmic signal, which is a common signal type in animal courtship (Mowles and Ord, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to comparative work on animal courtship signals.

claim: Signal speed is an important feature that conveys information and reshapes receiver behavior in courtship displays.
source: These displays convey information through multiple component signals, but one of particular importance in reshaping a receiver's behavior is signal speed (Schuppe and Fuxjager, 2018; Ord et al., 2007; Podos, 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies on signal speed in courtship.

claim: Females in golden-collared manakins discriminate millisecond-scale differences in displays and prefer to mate with males that display faster.
source: Although the degree to which roll-snap speed itself is sexually selected remains unknown, previous studies in golden-collared manakins show that females discriminate millisecond-scale differences in other displays and prefer to mate with males that display faster (Barske et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a study on female preferences in golden-collared manakins.

claim: The speed with which a male hits his wings together likely functions as an important courtship signal that is subject to strong sexual selection.
source: Therefore, the speed with which a male hits his wings together likely functions as an important courtship signal that is subject to strong sexual selection.
evidence: The claim is inferred from prior evidence about female preferences for display speed in related behaviors.

claim: Skeletal muscle speed is constrained by performance trade-offs, such as one between speed and endurance.
source: However, disruptive selection may not be able to freely drive sister species to exhibit opposite patterns of directional selection for this trait, largely because the speed with which skeletal muscles control wing movements is constrained by important performance trade-offs, such as one between speed and endurance (Vanhooydonck et al., 2014; Wilson et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies on muscle performance trade-offs.

claim: The bearded manakins' most recent common ancestor occupied a geographic range similar to that of the western population of extant white-bearded manakins.
source: The model output (Figure 1b) shows that the bearded manakins' most recent common ancestor occupied a geographic range similar to that of the western population of extant white-bearded manakins, giving rise to this species before migrating west across the Isthmus of Panama (Video 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by phylogeographic modeling results shown in Figure 1b.

claim: Golden-collared manakins emerged in a geographic range that overlapped between 49% and 73% (95% credible intervals) with that of the final common ancestor to both white-collared and orange-collared manakins.
source: Golden-collared manakins were the next to split off, emerging in a geographic range that overlapped between 49% and 73% (95% credible intervals) with that of the final common ancestor to both white-collared and orange-collared manakins.
evidence: The claim is supported by phylogeographic modeling data.

claim: Wide-ranging ancestral overlap is consistent with speciation occurring in sympatry, typically considered to occur when ranges overlap ≥25%.
source: This wide-ranging ancestral overlap is therefore consistent with speciation occurring in sympatry, typically considered to occur when ranges overlap ≥25% (Seddon, 2005; Cooney et al., 2017; Tobias et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by data on range overlap and citations defining sympatric speciation thresholds.

claim: Modern bearded manakins are mostly allopatric.
source: Furthermore, because modern bearded manakins are mostly allopatric (Figure 1c), geographic isolation of these birds likely followed their diversification, rather than preceding it.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1c depicting present-day species ranges.

claim: Geographic isolation of bearded manakins likely followed their diversification, rather than preceding it.
source: Furthermore, because modern bearded manakins are mostly allopatric (Figure 1c), geographic isolation of these birds likely followed their diversification, rather than preceding it.
evidence: The claim is inferred from phylogeographic data showing ancestral sympatry and current allopatry.

claim: Golden-collared and white-collared manakins hybridize readily in a small region of range overlap in Panama.
source: This is consistent with previous work in golden-collared and white-collared manakins, which hybridize readily in a small region of range overlap in Panama (Parsons et al., 1993).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a study documenting hybridization.

claim: In the hybrid zone, directional selection for plumage ornaments is strong enough for golden-collared manakin traits to cross the hybrid zone and introgress into the white-collared manakin population.
source: In the hybrid zone, directional selection for plumage ornaments is strong enough for golden-collared manakin traits to cross the hybrid zone and introgress into the white-collared manakin population (Parsons et al., 1993; McDonald et al., 2001; Brumfield et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies on introgression in the hybrid zone.

claim: Whole-genome analysis of golden-collared and white-collared manakins finds high rates of introgression and genetic differentiation at a wide range of unrelated loci.
source: Moreover, whole-genome analysis of the two species finds high rates of introgression and genetic differentiation at a wide range of unrelated loci, which is consistent with an evolutionary history characterized by reproductive isolation following adaptive divergence in various traits (Parchman et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a genomic study.

claim: High rates of introgression and genetic differentiation are consistent with an evolutionary history characterized by reproductive isolation following adaptive divergence in various traits.
source: Moreover, whole-genome analysis of the two species finds high rates of introgression and genetic differentiation at a wide range of unrelated loci, which is consistent with an evolutionary history characterized by reproductive isolation following adaptive divergence in various traits (Parchman et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is inferred from genomic data cited in the manuscript.

claim: Mechanisms other than those linked to geographic isolation likely help drive rapid speciation in the bearded manakin genus.
source: Thus, mechanisms other than those linked to geographic isolation likely help drive rapid speciation in the genus.
evidence: The claim is inferred from evidence of sympatric speciation and hybridization.

claim: Roll-snap speed differed significantly among bearded manakin species.
source: Speed differed significantly among the species (Figure 2a; F3,146=9.203, p<0.0001), with golden-collared manakins producing the fastest roll-snaps, white-bearded and white-collared manakins (no ancestral overlap) both producing intermediate speed roll-snaps, and orange-collared manakins producing the slowest roll-snaps.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of acoustic data shown in Figure 2a.

claim: Golden-collared manakins produce the fastest roll-snaps among bearded manakin species.
source: Speed differed significantly among the species (Figure 2a; F3,146=9.203, p<0.0001), with golden-collared manakins producing the fastest roll-snaps, white-bearded and white-collared manakins (no ancestral overlap) both producing intermediate speed roll-snaps, and orange-collared manakins producing the slowest roll-snaps.
evidence: The claim is supported by acoustic data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 2a.

claim: Orange-collared manakins produce the slowest roll-snaps among bearded manakin species.
source: Speed differed significantly among the species (Figure 2a; F3,146=9.203, p<0.0001), with golden-collared manakins producing the fastest roll-snaps, white-bearded and white-collared manakins (no ancestral overlap) both producing intermediate speed roll-snaps, and orange-collared manakins producing the slowest roll-snaps.
evidence: The claim is supported by acoustic data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 2a.

claim: The magnitude of mean differences in roll-snap speed is relatively small overall (<5 Hz).
source: The magnitude of mean differences is relatively small overall (<5 Hz), but also reflects larger differences in the upper range of display speed.
evidence: The claim is supported by acoustic data analysis.

claim: The fastest roll-snap observed in white-collared manakins (61 Hz) falls within the interquartile range of the golden-collared manakin's speed distribution [55.9,61.1].
source: For example, the fastest roll-snap observed in white-collared manakins (61 Hz) falls within the interquartile range of the golden-collared manakin's speed distribution [55.9,61.1].
evidence: The claim is supported by acoustic data analysis.

claim: Phenotypic constraints typically impact trait evolution by restricting the extremes of a distribution.
source: Because phenotypic constraints typically impact trait evolution by restricting the extremes of a distribution (Wilkins et al., 2013), this suggests that shifting constraint space may underlie differences in speed.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a study on phenotypic constraints.

claim: Roll-snap length in all four bearded manakin species was statistically indistinguishable.
source: At the same time, we found that roll snap length in all four species was statistically indistinguishable (Figure 2b; F3,153=0.229, p=0.876).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of acoustic data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: The roll-snap diverged among bearded manakin species exclusively in terms of signal speed, but not in terms of the total number of snaps.
source: Therefore, the roll-snap diverged among species exclusively in terms of signal speed (i.e. snap repetition rate), but not in terms of the total number of snaps.
evidence: The claim is supported by acoustic data showing species differences in speed but not length.

claim: If females attend to differences in roll-snap speed, conspecific mate preference should be reinforced by divergent roll-snap speeds.
source: Therefore, if females attend to differences in roll-snap speed as they do with other signals (Barske et al., 2011), conspecific mate preference should be reinforced by divergent roll-snap speeds (McDonald, 1989).
evidence: The claim is inferred from data on display divergence and citations on female preferences and assortative mating.

claim: The data are consistent with a model in which phenotypic divergence among sympatric populations plays a role in supporting assortative mating.
source: Our data are thus consistent with a model in which phenotypic divergence among sympatric populations plays a role in supporting assortative mating (Servedio, 2016; Kopp et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is inferred from data on sympatric speciation and display divergence, supported by citations to theoretical models.

claim: At the uppermost testable quantile (τ = 0.9), a trade-off between speed and length was detected in both golden-collared and white-collared manakins.
source: Indeed, at the uppermost testable quantile (τ = 0.9), we detected this trade-off in both golden-collared (Figure 3a; t = -4.03, p<0.001) and white-collared manakins (Figure 3b; t = -2.76, p=0.007), but not in white-bearded (Figure 3c; t = -0.36, p=0.722) and orange-collared manakins (Figure 3d; t = -0.70 p=0.490).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantile regression analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: No trade-off between speed and length was detected in white-bearded and orange-collared manakins at the uppermost testable quantile.
source: Indeed, at the uppermost testable quantile (τ = 0.9), we detected this trade-off in both golden-collared (Figure 3a; t = -4.03, p<0.001) and white-collared manakins (Figure 3b; t = -2.76, p=0.007), but not in white-bearded (Figure 3c; t = -0.36, p=0.722) and orange-collared manakins (Figure 3d; t = -0.70 p=0.490).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantile regression analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: Roll-snaps are differentially constrained across bearded manakin species.
source: Roll-snaps are therefore differentially constrained across species.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantile regression data showing trade-offs in some species but not others.

claim: The negative linear relationship between speed and length is steeper in golden-collared manakins than in white-collared manakins.
source: This was indeed the case (F1,230=22.1, p=0.001), supporting the notion that performance costs to speed become greater as selection drives the evolution of the signal further into the constrained trait-space.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical comparison of quantile regression slopes.

claim: Performance costs to speed become greater as selection drives the evolution of the signal further into the constrained trait-space.
source: This was indeed the case (F1,230=22.1, p=0.001), supporting the notion that performance costs to speed become greater as selection drives the evolution of the signal further into the constrained trait-space.
evidence: The claim is inferred from data showing steeper trade-offs in the faster species.

claim: Nearly all golden-collared manakins (top 80% of the population) experience a cost to display speed given the signal's length.
source: Our data again support this idea, as nearly all golden-collared manakins (top 80% of the population) experience a cost to display speed (Table 2), given the signal's length (Figure 3a; at τ = 0.2: t = -2.95, p=0.004), whereas only the top 20% of white-collared manakins display fast enough to experience such a cost (Figure 3b; at τ = 0.8: t = -2.33, p=0.028).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantile regression analysis shown in Figure 3a and Table 2.

claim: Only the top 20% of white-collared manakins display fast enough to experience a cost to display speed.
source: Our data again support this idea, as nearly all golden-collared manakins (top 80% of the population) experience a cost to display speed (Table 2), given the signal's length (Figure 3a; at τ = 0.2: t = -2.95, p=0.004), whereas only the top 20% of white-collared manakins display fast enough to experience such a cost (Figure 3b; at τ = 0.8: t = -2.33, p=0.028).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantile regression analysis shown in Figure 3b.

claim: For golden-collared and white-collared manakins, the rate at which an individual snaps its wings together to display is influenced by the inverse relationship between speed and endurance.
source: Thus, for these two species, the rate at which an individual snaps its wings together to display is influenced by the inverse relationship between speed and endurance, with the effect of this constraint appearing greater in golden-collared manakins.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantile regression data showing speed-endurance trade-offs.

claim: The effect of the speed-endurance constraint appears greater in golden-collared manakins than in white-collared manakins.
source: Thus, for these two species, the rate at which an individual snaps its wings together to display is influenced by the inverse relationship between speed and endurance, with the effect of this constraint appearing greater in golden-collared manakins.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantile regression data showing a steeper trade-off affecting more individuals in golden-collared manakins.

claim: The scapulohumeralis caudalis muscle (SH) is the primary actuator of the roll-snap in bearded manakins.
source: In bearded manakins, the scapulohumeralis caudalis muscle (SH, Figure 4a) is the primary actuator of the roll-snap—it contracts when a male's wings are raised vertically above its back, causing the wrists to collide (snap) over the axial mid-line (Fuxjager et al., 2017a).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a study on the biomechanics of the roll-snap.

claim: The SH muscle contracts when a male's wings are raised vertically above its back, causing the wrists to collide (snap) over the axial mid-line.
source: In bearded manakins, the scapulohumeralis caudalis muscle (SH, Figure 4a) is the primary actuator of the roll-snap—it contracts when a male's wings are raised vertically above its back, causing the wrists to collide (snap) over the axial mid-line (Fuxjager et al., 2017a).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a study on the biomechanics of the roll-snap.

claim: The SH is a flight muscle, acting as a 'strut' during powered locomotion by rotating and retracting the wing.
source: Otherwise, the SH is a flight muscle, acting as a 'strut' during powered locomotion by rotating and retracting the wing (Dial, 1992).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a study on avian flight muscle function.

claim: Bearded manakins maintain an extremely fast SH, likely due to selection for a fast display.
source: Past work shows that bearded manakins maintain an extremely fast SH, likely due to selection for a fast display (Barske et al., 2011; Fuxjager et al., 2016a; Fuxjager et al., 2017b); thus, one might expect that the evolution of SH speed contends with a decrease in endurance.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies on SH muscle performance and sexual selection.

claim: Golden-collared manakins maintain an extremely fast SH muscle that relaxes more quickly at high frequencies than it does in white-collared manakins.
source: Our results confirmed previous work (Fuxjager et al., 2016a) by indicating that golden-collared manakins maintain an extremely fast SH—that is, this muscle relaxes more quickly at high frequencies than it does in white-collared manakins (Figure 4c; model difference: F3,49=15.2, p<0.001).
evidence: The claim is supported by in situ muscle recording data shown in Figure 4c.

claim: The SH muscle maintains a significantly greater half-relaxation frequency in the golden-collared manakin than in the white-collared manakin.
source: The muscle therefore also maintains a significantly greater half-relaxation frequency in the golden-collared manakin, which is the maximum frequency at which the muscle contracts and relaxes at 50% of its predicted functional range (Figure 4d; F1,49=79.8, p<0.001).
evidence: The claim is supported by in situ muscle recording data shown in Figure 4d.

claim: When stimulated at ≥80 Hz, the golden-collared manakin SH's percent relaxation significantly declined with each twitch.
source: However, when stimulated at ≥80 Hz, its percent relaxation significantly declined with each twitch (Figure 5a and Table 3; F1,12=18.7, p=0.005 at 80 Hz; F1,12=33.9, p<0.001 at 90 Hz; F1,12=22.8, p=0.003 at 100 Hz).
evidence: The claim is supported by in situ muscle recording data shown in Figure 5a and Table 3.

claim: The level of relaxation in the golden-collared manakin SH dropped from around 75–100% during the first contraction to around 20–50% as the stimulation train progressed at high frequencies.
source: Indeed, we find that the level of relaxation dropped from around 75–100% during the first contraction to around 20–50% as the stimulation train progressed.
evidence: The claim is supported by in situ muscle recording data.

claim: In the white-collared manakin, percent relaxation of the SH never changed across any of the stimulation trains.
source: By contrast, in the white-collared manakin, percent relaxation of the SH never changed across any of the stimulation trains (Figure 5b and Table 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by in situ muscle recording data shown in Figure 5b and Table 3.

claim: The golden-collared manakin SH experiences a form of 'rapid fatigue' when stimulated at especially fast frequencies.
source: These data therefore suggest that the golden-collared manakin SH experiences a form of 'rapid fatigue' when stimulated at especially fast frequencies.
evidence: The claim is inferred from muscle recording data showing declining relaxation at high stimulation frequencies.

claim: The SH performance decline in golden-collared manakins contrasts with fatigue as it is normally discussed, where the latter is typically defined as a decrease in speed and force production over periods of time greater than the fractions-of-a-second shown in this study.
source: This performance attribute contrasts with fatigue as it is normally discussed, where the latter is typically defined as a decrease in speed and force production over periods of time greater than the fractions-of-a-second that we show herein (Wilson et al., 2002; Allen et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations defining standard muscle fatigue and comparison to the observed rapid decline.

claim: The ability to resist 'rapid fatigue' qualifies as a form of muscle endurance.
source: Nonetheless, we expect that the ability to resist this 'rapid fatigue' similarly qualifies as a form of muscle endurance per se (the ability to resist fatigue; Wilson et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the definition of endurance and the observed performance decline, supported by a citation.

claim: SH performance declines in golden-collared manakins as stimulation frequency increases, but not in white-collared manakins.
source: Note that SH performance—as measured by the SH's ability to resist 'rapid fatigue' during high frequency stimulations—declines in golden-collared manakins (F1,6=27.7, p=0.004, R2 = 0.82), but not in white-collared manakins (F1,7=0.15, p=0.711).
evidence: The claim is supported by regression analysis of muscle performance data shown in Figure 5c.

claim: For the golden-collared manakin, the upper confidence limit of the regression line crosses 0 at ≈60 Hz, which represents the relative speed at which the trade-off with endurance should begin to manifest.
source: Importantly, for the golden-collared manakin, we show that the upper confidence limit of this regression line crosses 0 at ≈60 Hz—a value that represents the relative speed at which the trade-off with endurance should begin to manifest.
evidence: The claim is supported by regression analysis of muscle performance data.

claim: The speed at which the trade-off with endurance begins to manifest (≈60 Hz) roughly corresponds to the golden-collared manakin's average roll-snap speed of 58.4 Hz.
source: This roughly correspond to the species' average roll-snap speed, which is 58.4 Hz (Figures 2a and 5c).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of muscle performance data and acoustic data.

claim: Sexual selection in golden-collared manakins has likely driven the evolution of the roll-snap to its maximal speed, such that it is produced at the SH's performance limit due to the tissue's intrinsic trade-off with endurance.
source: Thus, sexual selection in golden-collared manakins has likely driven the evolution of the roll-snap to its maximal speed, such that it is produced at the SH's performance limit due to the tissue's intrinsic trade-off with endurance.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the correspondence between muscle performance limits and display speed.

claim: Male golden-collared manakins produce significantly shorter roll-snaps when they are at or above 60 Hz, compared to less than 60 Hz.
source: Further support for this idea comes from a subsequent analysis, in which we found that male golden-collared manakin produce significantly shorter roll-snaps when they are at or above 60 Hz, compared to less than 60 Hz (β = −4.32, F1,119=46.7, p<0.001; Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of acoustic data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: For both golden-collared and white-collared manakins, shortening and lengthening duration remained consistent during the stimulation trains.
source: Both measures showed considerable variation, but for both species we found no significant changes within the twitch series (pmin = 0.20; Figure 6). This indicates that shortening and lengthening duration remained consistent during the stimulation trains.
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of contraction timing data shown in Figure 6.

claim: The overall 'rapid fatigue' response in golden-collared manakins is likely a result of decreased capacity for relaxation.
source: Nonetheless, in the golden-collared manakin, we know that percent relaxation declines at high stimulation frequencies in this same timeframe. Thus, the overall 'rapid fatigue' response is likely a result of decreased capacity for relaxation, pointing to processes underlying this event as a potential limiter of muscle performance.
evidence: The claim is inferred from data showing declining relaxation without changes in contraction/relaxation timing.

claim: The 'rapid fatigue' response may be linked to constraints on calcium buffering and/or re-uptake mechanisms, given they play an important role in setting muscle relaxation rates.
source: This may be linked to constraints on calcium buffering and/or re-uptake mechanisms, given they play an important role in setting muscle relaxation rates (Syme and Josephson, 2002; Rome et al., 1996).
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on inference from muscle performance data and citations on calcium cycling in muscle.

claim: The phenotype favored by selection will evolve following directional selection until it is impeded by the underlying rate-limiting mechanism.
source: Regardless of which cellular mechanism ultimately limits SH performance in the golden-collared manakin, this is consistent with the fundamental framework of selection contending with constraint—the phenotype favored by selection (in this case, display speed) will evolve following directional selection until it is impeded by the underlying rate-limiting mechanism.
evidence: The claim is based on established evolutionary theory and inference from the data.

claim: The golden-collared manakin SH has been modified to allow the muscle to sustain rapid contraction-relaxation cycling, but different components of myocytic machinery have likely evolved in a mismatched fashion.
source: In this case, it appears that the golden-collared manakin SH has been modified to allow the muscle to sustain rapid contraction-relaxation cycling, but different components of myocytic machinery have likely evolved in a mismatched fashion.
evidence: The claim is inferred from muscle performance data showing rapid contraction but declining relaxation.

claim: Further evolutionary elaboration of the roll-snap speed would likely require modifications to the calcium handling properties, alongside other adaptations for the performance of this signal in bearded manakins.
source: Further evolutionary elaboration of the roll-snap speed would likely require modifications to the calcium handling properties, alongside other adaptations for the performance of this signal in bearded manakins (Friscia et al., 2016; Fuxjager et al., 2016b; Fuxjager et al., 2016c).
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on inference from muscle performance data and citations on muscle adaptations.

claim: Limitations to muscular calcium handling are not typically associated with the speed-endurance trade-off, which is often considered to result from muscle fiber type composition.
source: Notably, limitations to muscular calcium handling are not typically associated with the speed-endurance trade-off, which is often considered to result from muscle fiber type composition (Rivero et al., 1993; Komi, 1984; Esbjörnsson et al., 1993).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations on the typical mechanisms underlying speed-endurance trade-offs.

claim: The discrepancy between the observed 'rapid fatigue' and standard muscle fatigue is likely the result of differences in the timescale over which performance is depleted.
source: This discrepancy is likely the result of differences between the so-called 'rapid fatigue' we observe and the more standard muscle fatigue that occurs when performance is depleted after prolonged muscle use.
evidence: The claim is inferred from comparison of the observed rapid decline with standard definitions of fatigue.

claim: Bearded manakin species evolved in a geographic scenario characterized by considerable range overlap.
source: Our results show that the species in this complex evolved in a geographic scenario characterized by considerable range overlap, which means that that rapid speciation was likely facilitated by strong assortative mating (Servedio, 2016; Kopp et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by phylogeographic modeling data.

claim: Rapid speciation in bearded manakins was likely facilitated by strong assortative mating.
source: Our results show that the species in this complex evolved in a geographic scenario characterized by considerable range overlap, which means that that rapid speciation was likely facilitated by strong assortative mating (Servedio, 2016; Kopp et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is inferred from phylogeographic data showing sympatric speciation, supported by citations to theoretical models.

claim: Bearded manakin divergence took place after ancestral populations migrated northwest out of Amazonia, across the Andes, and along the Isthmus of Panama.
source: Bearded manakin divergence took place after ancestral populations migrated northwest out of Amazonia, across the Andes, and along the Isthmus of Panama.
evidence: The claim is supported by phylogeographic modeling data.

claim: When the golden-collared manakin first diverged from its shared common ancestor with white- and orange-collared manakins, its range spanned the entire isthmus.
source: When the golden-collared manakin first diverged from its shared common ancestor with white- and orange-collared manakins, its range spanned the entire isthmus.
evidence: The claim is supported by phylogeographic modeling data.

claim: As bearded manakin species split, their roll-snap speeds also diverged for the three taxa that were ancestrally sympatric.
source: As the species split, their roll-snap speeds also diverged for the three taxa that were ancestrally sympatric, and their ranges also began contracting to generate the (mostly) allopatric configuration seen today (Video 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by acoustic data and phylogeographic modeling.

claim: Bearded manakin ranges began contracting to generate the (mostly) allopatric configuration seen today.
source: As the species split, their roll-snap speeds also diverged for the three taxa that were ancestrally sympatric, and their ranges also began contracting to generate the (mostly) allopatric configuration seen today (Video 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by phylogeographic modeling data.

claim: The golden-collared manakin's roll-snap increased in speed during speciation.
source: Specifically, we found that the golden-collared manakin's roll-snap increased in speed, presumably at the same time as its SH was modified to support the especially rapid contraction-relaxation cycling that was necessarily to generate the movements that make up this behavior.
evidence: The claim is supported by acoustic data and muscle performance data.

claim: The golden-collared manakin's SH was modified to support the especially rapid contraction-relaxation cycling necessary to generate the roll-snap behavior.
source: Specifically, we found that the golden-collared manakin's roll-snap increased in speed, presumably at the same time as its SH was modified to support the especially rapid contraction-relaxation cycling that was necessarily to generate the movements that make up this behavior.
evidence: The claim is inferred from muscle performance data showing faster contraction-relaxation cycling in golden-collared manakins.

claim: The species with the fastest display, the golden-collared manakin, also has the fastest SH muscle.
source: We then show that this evolutionary pattern is explained by contraction-relaxation cycling kinetics in the skeletal muscle that actuates the roll-snap display—namely the SH. Thus, the species with the fastest display, the golden-collared manakin, also has the fastest SH.
